text: Scope is the rulebook for where a variable exists and which code can see it.
Here x is global, defined at the top level of the file, visible everywhere below.
But inside show, we assign x again — that creates a separate local variable, living only in the function.
[chuckle] So inside prints local, while outside still prints global — they never touched each other.
To actually change a global from inside a function, you must declare it with the global keyword.
[sniff] Now bump really does increment the module-level counter, and the change sticks after it returns.
Python resolves every name using a rule called LEGB — Local, then Enclosing, then Global, then Built-in.
Here inner finds msg in the enclosing function's scope, one level out, and prints it.
[groan] Understanding scope saves you from the confusing bugs where a variable mysteriously isn't what you expected.
